# Dynamic Float Array in C

Here's a complete, safe, and well-documented C implementation of a dynamic array of floats with resizing capability:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

typedef struct {
    float *data;
    size_t size;
    size_t capacity;
} FloatArray;

// Initialize the array
bool float_array_init(FloatArray *arr, size_t initial_capacity) {
    if (initial_capacity == 0) {
        initial_capacity = 8;
    }

    arr->data = (float *)malloc(initial_capacity * sizeof(float));
    if (arr->data == NULL) {
        return false;
    }

    arr->size = 0;
    arr->capacity = initial_capacity;
    return true;
}

// Add a value to the array
bool float_array_add(FloatArray *arr, float value) {
    if (arr->size >= arr->capacity) {
        size_t new_capacity = arr->capacity * 2;
        float *new_data = (float *)realloc(arr->data, new_capacity * sizeof(float));

        if (new_data == NULL) {
            return false;
        }

        arr->data = new_data;
        arr->capacity = new_capacity;
    }

    arr->data[arr->size++] = value;
    return true;
}

// Get the size of the array
size_t float_array_size(const FloatArray *arr) {
    return arr->size;
}

// Get value at index (with bounds checking)
bool float_array_get(const FloatArray *arr, size_t index, float *value) {
    if (index >= arr->size) {
        return false;
    }

    *value = arr->data[index];
    return true;
}

// Set value at index (with bounds checking)
bool float_array_set(FloatArray *arr, size_t index, float value) {
    if (index >= arr->size) {
        return false;
    }

    arr->data[index] = value;
    return true;
}

// Remove the last element
bool float_array_remove_last(FloatArray *arr, float *value) {
    if (arr->size == 0) {
        return false;
    }

    *value = arr->data[--arr->size];
    return true;
}

// Free the array memory
void float_array_free(FloatArray *arr) {
    if (arr->data != NULL) {
        free(arr->data);
        arr->data = NULL;
        arr->size = 0;
        arr->capacity = 0;
    }
}

// Optional: Print array contents
void float_array_print(const FloatArray *arr) {
    printf("[");
    for (size_t i = 0; i < arr->size; i++) {
        printf("%g", arr->data[i]);
        if (i < arr->size - 1) {
            printf(", ");
        }
    }
    printf("]\n");
}

// Example usage
int main() {
    FloatArray arr;

    if (!float_array_init(&arr, 0)) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize array\n");
        return 1;
    }

    // Add elements
    float_array_add(&arr, 1.5f);
    float_array_add(&arr, 2.7f);
    float_array_add(&arr, 3.14f);
    float_array_add(&arr, 42.0f);
    float_array_add(&arr, 99.9f);

    // Print array
    printf("Current array: ");
    float_array_print(&arr);

    // Access element
    float value;
    if (float_array_get(&arr, 2, &value)) {
        printf("Element at index 2: %f\n", value);
    }

    // Modify element
    float_array_set(&arr, 0, 10.0f);
    printf("After modification: ");
    float_array_print(&arr);

    // Remove last element
    float_array_remove_last(&arr, &value);
    printf("After removal: ");
    float_array_print(&arr);

    // Clean up
    float_array_free(&arr);

    return 0;
}
```

## Key Features

- ✅ **Dynamic Resizing**: Capacity doubles when full
- ✅ **Memory Safety**: Proper allocation and deallocation
- ✅ **Bounds Checking**: Safe access with return status
- ✅ **Convenient API**: Add, get, set, remove, print
- ✅ **Example Usage**: Demonstrates all functions


Here's a JavaScript example that sorts an array of objects by a numeric field called `count`. It demonstrates both ascending and descending order using the `sort()` method with a custom compare function.

```javascript
// Example array of objects with a 'count' field
const items = [
  { name: 'Item A', count: 6 },
  { name: 'Item B', count: 13 },
  { name: 'Item C', count: 19 }
];

// Sort by 'count' in ascending order
const sortedAscending = [...items].sort((a, b) => a.count - b.count);

// Sort by 'count' in descending order
const sortedDescending = [...items].sort((a, b) => b.count - a.count);

// Output results
console.log('Original:');
console.log(items);

console.log('\nSorted Ascending (6, 13, 19):');
console.log(sortedAscending);

console.log('\nSorted Descending (19, 13, 6):');
console.log(sortedDescending);
```

**Explanation:**
- The `sort()` method is used with a compare function that subtracts the `count` values.
- `[...items]` creates a shallow copy of the array to avoid mutating the original.
- `a.count - b.count` sorts in ascending order.
- `b.count - a.count` sorts in descending order.

This approach ensures the original array remains unchanged while providing sorted versions based on the `count` field.<|im_end|>
